source_evidence.observation: The standing problem is Ax=b with A in R^{n×n} nonsingular and 0≠b in R^n; the left and right preconditioners M_L and M_R are nonsingular.

Preconditioner applications use precision u_m, matrix-vector products with A use u_a, and the remaining MGS-GMRES operations use u_g. Flexible GMRES stores the computed preconditioned vectors in an additional basis Z_k.

The right path computes z_j=M^{-1}v_j, w_j=Az_j, y'_k=V_k y_k, and x_k=x_0+M^{-1}y'_k. The flexible replacement is x_k=x_0+Z_k y_k. Although flexible GMRES generally permits a varying preconditioner, this study fixes one M_R for every iteration.

The symbols u_m, u_a, and u_g denote either floating-point arithmetics or their unit roundoffs; Section 3 permits any such arithmetics whose unit roundoffs are substantially below 1. The paper imports the standard floating-point model and writes fl for a computed value.

The functions c(n,k) are unspecified low-degree polynomials. The symbols ≲ and ≈ discard negligible second-order terms, and much-greater-than is intended to dominate c(n,k) factors. Vector forward error is ||x_hat-x||_2/||x||_2. The paper defines 2-norm, Frobenius norm, κ_F, κ_2, and κ_{F,2}, then uses unqualified κ when it does not distinguish them.

source_evidence.anchor: Algorithm 2 and MGS least-squares error model
source_evidence.observation: Algorithm 2 forms C_k=M_L^{-1}A Z_tilde_k, forms b_tilde=M_L^{-1}b, solves the least-squares problem by MGS, Givens rotations, and a triangular solve, and forms x_k=Z_tilde_k y_k. The MGS least-squares perturbation result is imported from earlier work and requires the computed C_k not to be numerically singular.

The modular theorem assumes a full-rank search basis of increasing dimension and provides an existential k≤n with reciprocal smallest singular value and largest singular value of V_hat_k both at most 4/3. Its applicability also requires the modular error models and conditions (3.5)-(3.6).

For right preconditioning M_L=I and M_R≠I, equation (3.14) models every computed inverse-preconditioner application. Equation (3.15) defines rho_A^R. Theorem 3.3 assumes all five entries of (3.16) are much less than 1 and concludes the existential right-preconditioned bound (3.17). Remark 3 describes the last entry as likely pessimistic and offers (3.18) as an alternative condition.

Flexible GMRES uses one fixed M_R^{(j)}=M_R≠I for all j≤k and M_L=I, stores Z_hat_k, and forms the solution directly with it. Theorem 3.4 assumes the unchanged condition (3.16) and concludes (3.20). Remark 4 compares approximate bounds and notes the absence of the preconditioner-reapplication term; Remark 5 still identifies two requirements within (3.16) as likely pessimistic.

Appendix A imports and asserts a straightforward adaptation of an MGS result from reference [11]: for an increasing full-rank basis there is a dimension k≤n satisfying the augmented-matrix condition (A.1) and the conditioning bounds (3.7). This k is selected for Theorem 3.1.
The proof introduces the mathematical artifact x_hat_k^R=M_R Z_tilde_k y_hat_k and subsequently divides by its norm and squared norm.
The paper says expressions involving M_R Z_tilde_k are well-defined because M_R is nonsingular and Z_tilde_k is full-rank, but it does not separately state that y_hat_k or x_hat_k^R is nonzero.

Appendix C imports the standard matrix-vector rounding bound, defines Z_tilde_k by absorbing A-product roundoff into an analysis-only basis, and thereby sets epsilon_c=0. It says the proof must establish the modular conditions at any k satisfying (3.7).

For right GMRES the first-order solution perturbation contains the reapplication error, the V_hat_k y_hat_k multiplication error, the original preconditioner-application basis error, and the absorbed A-product error. These yield epsilon_x proportional to u_m eta_R κ(M_R)+u_g κ(M_R)+u_a κ(A)rho_A^R.
Appendix C derives lower and upper bounds for A Z_tilde_k and uses condition (3.16) to establish modular condition (3.5); these are proof deductions rather than additional theorem assumptions.

source_evidence.anchor: Appendix C conclusion, equation (C.15), and Appendix D opening
source_evidence.observation: Appendix C states that the modular conditions hold for any k satisfying (3.7) under Theorem 3.3's assumptions and then invokes Theorem 3.1's existential dimension. Appendix D reuses specified Appendix C relations and the same proof of condition (3.5).

Flexible solution formation gives the first-order perturbation Δx=(ΔZ_k^{(3)}-ΔZ_k^{(2)})y_hat_k and epsilon_x proportional to u_g κ(M_R)+u_a κ(A)rho_A^R. Substitution into Theorem 3.1 produces (3.20).

binders: Common exact data are a dimension n, a nonsingular A in R^{n×n}, a nonzero b in R^n, and the exact solution x of Ax=b. (PDF p. 2, eq. (1.1).)
The right-preconditioned scope uses one nonsingular nonidentity M_R in R^{n×n}, M_L≡I, and one right-preconditioned MGS-GMRES computation. (PDF p. 2, eq. (1.2); PDF p. 11, Section 3.3 opening.)

The flexible scope also uses M_L≡I and exactly one fixed nonsingular nonidentity preconditioner, explicitly M_R^{(j)}=M_R for every j≤k; it does not quantify a separate preconditioner per column. (PDF p. 12, Section 3.4 opening.)
For each j≤k, the model binds an application error ΔM_R^{(j)} and a scalar eta_R through equation (3.14). (PDF p. 11, eq. (3.14).)

At a candidate k, V_hat_k is the computed Krylov basis, z_hat_j=fl(M_R^{-1}v_hat_j), Z_hat_k=[z_hat_1,...,z_hat_k], y_hat_k is the computed least-squares vector, and x_hat_k is the computed solution. (PDF p. 11, eqs. (3.14)-(3.15); PDF p. 7, Algorithm 2.)
Theorems 3.3 and 3.4 each introduce their own existential iteration k≤n; neither theorem states that its witness equals the other's witness. (PDF p. 11, Theorem 3.3; PDF p. 12, Theorem 3.4.)
hypotheses: The inverse-preconditioner application model is fl(M_R^{-1}v_hat_j)=(M_R^{-1}+ΔM_R^{(j)})v_hat_j with ||ΔM_R^{(j)}||_F≤c(n,k)u_m eta_R||M_R^{-1}||_F for j≤k. (PDF p. 11, eq. (3.14).)

Successive products A M_R^{-1}v_hat_j apply M_R^{-1} in precision u_m and A in precision u_a; MGS and the other GMRES work use u_g. (PDF p. 3, paragraph introducing Algorithm 1; PDF p. 11, Section 3.3.)
Theorem 3.3 assumes max(u_g κ(A M_R^{-1}), u_g κ(M_R), u_m eta_R κ(M_R), u_a κ(A)rho_A^R, u_a κ(A M_R^{-1})κ(M_R))≪1. (PDF p. 11, eq. (3.16) and Theorem 3.3.)
Theorem 3.4 explicitly assumes that the same complete condition (3.16) is satisfied; it does not delete the u_m eta_R κ(M_R) entry or any other entry. (PDF p. 12, Theorem 3.4.)
The flexible theorem inherits the same column-generation model (3.14) and identical successive A M_R^{-1}v_hat_j computations as the right theorem. (PDF p. 12, first two paragraphs of Section 3.4.)

Neither theorem assumes eta_R or rho_A^R is itself an order-one constant; only the displayed products containing them are constrained by (3.16). The order-one treatment appears later as a simplification, not in Theorems 3.3-3.4. (PDF p. 11, Theorem 3.3; PDF p. 12, Theorem 3.4 and beginning of Section 3.5.)
conclusions: Right theorem: there exists k≤n such that ||x_hat_k-x||_2/||x||_2 ≲ c(n,k)(u_g κ(A M_R^{-1})κ(M_R)+u_m eta_R κ(M_R)+u_a κ(A)rho_A^R). (PDF p. 11, eq. (3.17).)
Flexible theorem: there exists k≤n such that ||x_hat_k-x||_2/||x||_2 ≲ c(n,k)(u_g κ(A M_R^{-1})κ(M_R)+u_a κ(A)rho_A^R). (PDF p. 12, eq. (3.20).)

Theorem 3.4 does not require as a premise that Theorem 3.3's right-preconditioned existential conclusion has already been established; it reuses the condition and proof machinery directly. (PDF p. 12, text before Theorem 3.4; PDF pp. 44-45, Appendix D.)

Remark 4 records omission of the explicit u_m eta_R κ(M_R) reapplication contribution from the flexible approximate bound; it is not an exact algebraic identity and does not formally weaken condition (3.16). (PDF p. 12, Remark 4; PDF p. 45, eq. (D.2).)
definitions_and_conventions: rho_A^R=|| |Z_hat_k| |y_hat_k| ||_2/||Z_hat_k y_hat_k||_2, where absolute values are componentwise and Z_hat_k consists of the computed preconditioned columns. (PDF p. 11, eq. (3.15).)
eta_R is only described as a scalar quantifying the magnitude of inverse-preconditioner application error through (3.14). (PDF p. 11, text following eq. (3.14).)
c(n,k) denotes an unspecified low-degree polynomial in n and k used to collect worst-case constants. (PDF p. 6, Section 2 conventions.)
The notation ≲, like ≈, signals that negligible second-order terms have been dropped; it is not introduced as an exact ordered relation with a specified constant. (PDF p. 6, Section 2 conventions.)
The notation ≪ is qualitative much-less-than; the paper's reciprocal convention says a much-greater quantity is taken to dominate an additional c(n,k) factor. (PDF p. 6, Section 2 conventions.)

Z_hat_k is algorithmically formed and stored, whereas Z_tilde_k in Appendix C is an inaccessible analysis artifact chosen to absorb A-product rounding errors. (PDF p. 41, eq. (C.2) and following paragraph.)
implicit_context: The existential k is supplied by Theorem 3.1's MGS mechanism, not by a convergence or residual-tolerance assumption: Appendix A imports from reference [11] an existential dimension satisfying (A.1) and the conditioning bounds (3.7). (PDF p. 36, Appendix A opening and eq. (A.1).)

The imported MGS facts include the perturbed least-squares characterization and the requirement that the computed least-squares matrix not be numerically singular; the paper does not rederive those facts locally. (PDF p. 7, MGS least-squares discussion.)
Theorem 3.1 additionally assumes a full-rank search basis of increasing dimension and modular error conditions (3.2)-(3.6). (PDF pp. 7-8, error models and Theorem 3.1.)

Appendix C locally constructs Z_tilde_k, sets epsilon_c=0 by absorbing A roundoff, sets epsilon_b=0 because M_L=I, derives epsilon_x, and verifies conditions (3.5)-(3.6) under (3.16). (PDF pp. 41-44, Appendix C.)
Appendix D locally changes only solution formation, reuses equations (C.2), (C.5), (C.7), (C.8), and (C.10), and reuses Appendix C's verification of condition (3.5). (PDF pp. 44-45, Appendix D.)

Remark 3 says the last entry u_a κ(A M_R^{-1})κ(M_R)≪1 is likely pessimistic and could be replaced by c(n,k)u_g κ(A Z_tilde_k)≪1; the displayed Theorem 3.3 nevertheless retains (3.16). (PDF p. 11, Remark 3 and eq. (3.18).)
Remark 5 calls the u_m eta_R κ(M_R) and u_a κ(A M_R^{-1})κ(M_R) requirements likely pessimistic for flexible GMRES, but Theorem 3.4 itself still assumes all of (3.16). (PDF p. 12, Remark 5.)
statement.algorithm_linkage: Algorithm 1 right computes each z_j=M_R^{-1}v_j in u_m, each A z_j in u_a, the MGS least-squares work in u_g, then computes y'_k=V_k y_k in u_g and reapplies M_R^{-1} in u_m to form x_k=x_0+M_R^{-1}y'_k. Flexible GMRES has the same Arnoldi/MGS prefix with one fixed M_R, stores Z_k, and instead forms x_k=x_0+Z_k y_k directly in u_g. Algorithm 2 abstracts these as M_L=I, C_k=A Z_tilde_k, b_tilde=b with no computation, and solution formation x_k=Z_tilde_k y_k; Appendices C and D supply the respective links between the actual and analysis bases. (PDF p. 4, Algorithm 1 and following paragraph; PDF p. 7, Algorithm 2; PDF p. 11, Section 3.3; PDF p. 12, Section 3.4.)
numerical_model: The paper imports the standard floating-point model, uses fl for computed expressions, and permits generic arithmetics u_m, u_a, and u_g whose unit roundoffs are substantially below 1. (PDF p. 5, Section 2.)
Matrix-vector rounding is imported through the componentwise relation |ΔA^{(j)}|≲c(n,k)u_a|A|; Appendix C uses it in (C.1)-(C.2). (PDF p. 41, eqs. (C.1)-(C.2).)
Right solution formation has the first-order relation Δx=(ΔM_R^{(x)}V_hat_k+M_R^{-1}ΔV_k-ΔZ_k^{(1)}-ΔZ_k^{(2)})y_hat_k after second-order terms are dropped. (PDF p. 42, eqs. (C.3)-(C.6).)
Flexible solution formation has fl(Z_hat_k y_hat_k)=(Z_hat_k+ΔZ_k^{(3)})y_hat_k with |ΔZ_k^{(3)}|≲c(n,k)u_g|Z_hat_k| and Δx=(ΔZ_k^{(3)}-ΔZ_k^{(2)})y_hat_k. (PDF p. 45, eq. (D.1).)

The MGS least-squares model, Givens-rotation behavior, and triangular-solve accuracy are imported from references [30] and [11], while their use inside Theorem 3.1 and the right/flexible perturbation propagation are local to this paper. (PDF p. 7, MGS discussion; PDF p. 36, Appendix A; PDF pp. 41-45, Appendices C-D.)
error_notions: The theorem conclusions concern normwise forward error ||x_hat_k-x||_2/||x||_2 for the original system, not backward error. (PDF p. 6, eq. (2.1); PDF pp. 11-12, eqs. (3.17) and (3.20).)
Appendix C's raw solution-formation bound is ||Δx||_2≲c(n,k)(u_m eta_R κ(M_R)+u_g κ(M_R)+u_a κ(A)rho_A^R)||Z_tilde_k y_hat_k||_2. (PDF p. 43, eq. (C.11).)
Appendix D's raw solution-formation bound is ||Δx||_2≲c(n,k)(u_g κ(M_R)+u_a κ(A)rho_A^R)||Z_tilde_k y_hat_k||_2. (PDF p. 45, eq. (D.2).)

The raw ΔZ and Δx relations in Appendices C-D are proof-derived first-order contributions, not extra assumptions listed by Theorems 3.3 or 3.4. (PDF pp. 41-45, Appendices C-D; PDF pp. 11-12, theorem statements.)

The final u_g κ(A M_R^{-1})κ(M_R) term also incorporates the MGS/least-squares contribution from Theorem 3.1; it is not merely the direct final matrix-vector-product error. (PDF p. 44, expressions for beta u_g and lambda epsilon_x; PDF p. 45, final substitution.)
norms: All displayed forward errors and rho_A^R use the vector 2-norm. (PDF p. 6, eq. (2.1); PDF p. 11, eq. (3.15).)
The perturbation model (3.14) bounds ΔM_R^{(j)} and M_R^{-1} in the Frobenius norm. (PDF p. 11, eq. (3.14).)

The paper defines κ_F(B)=||B^{-1}||_F||B||_F, κ_2(B)=sigma_max(B)/sigma_min(B), and κ_{F,2}(B)=||B||_F/sigma_min(B), but writes only κ in (3.16), (3.17), and (3.20). (PDF p. 6, norm conventions; PDF pp. 11-12, theorem formulas.)

Consequently, the theorem statements do not select one exact condition-number norm; the proofs mix singular-value and Frobenius-norm estimates and suppress the distinction through norm equivalence. (PDF p. 6, norm conventions; PDF pp. 42-44, Appendix C estimates.)
constants_and_indexing: The inverse-preconditioner model applies for every column index j≤k, and the flexible section fixes M_R^{(j)}=M_R over that whole prefix. (PDF p. 11, eq. (3.14); PDF p. 12, Section 3.4 opening.)

Each theorem's witness is an iteration/dimension k≤n; the source does not explicitly write a lower bound, though Algorithm 1 indexes iterations from j=1. (PDF p. 4, Algorithm 1; PDF pp. 11-12, Theorems 3.3-3.4.)

The MGS-selected k satisfies sigma_min(V_hat_k)^{-1}≤4/3 and sigma_max(V_hat_k)≤4/3, and, when k≤n-1, the imported augmented-matrix condition (A.1) holds for every phi>0. (PDF p. 36, eq. (A.1); PDF p. 8, eq. (3.7).)
In both (3.17) and (3.20), c(n,k) multiplies the entire parenthesized sum, not only its first term. (PDF p. 11, eq. (3.17); PDF p. 12, eq. (3.20).)

The visible condition (3.16) contains exactly five entries and no visible outer c(n,k), although c(n,k) occurs in the underlying application model and is absorbed by the paper's qualitative much-less-than convention. (PDF p. 11, eqs. (3.14) and (3.16); PDF p. 6, convention for much-greater-than.)
higher_order_terms: The relations marked ≲ or ≈ are first-order descriptions obtained by discarding terms called negligible and second order; the paper gives no explicit remainder term or universal comparison constant. (PDF p. 6, Section 2 conventions.)

Appendix C explicitly drops the product of final preconditioner-application and V_k-product errors in (C.3), and later uses (3.16) to discard second-order terms in rank and norm estimates. (PDF pp. 42-44, eqs. (C.3), (C.13)-(C.15).)
Appendix D inherits Appendix C's first-order reductions and derives another ≲ bound rather than an exact equality between the right and flexible errors. (PDF pp. 44-45, Appendix D.)
exceptional_values: The PDF invokes the standard floating-point model but does not explicitly state treatment of overflow, underflow, subnormals, infinities, NaNs, or invalid operations. (PDF p. 5, Section 2.)

Algorithm 1 and the theorem statements do not explicitly exclude zero Arnoldi normalization factors, MGS happy breakdown, or other divisions by zero; numerical nonsingularity is discussed only inside the imported modular analysis. (PDF p. 4, Algorithm 1; PDF pp. 7-8, MGS model and Theorem 3.1.)

A nonsingular A and nonzero b make the exact solution x nonzero, so the forward-error denominator is nonzero; no corresponding explicit nonzero assumption is stated for ||Z_hat_k y_hat_k||_2 in rho_A^R or ||x_hat_k^R||_2 in Appendix A. (PDF p. 2, eq. (1.1); PDF p. 11, eq. (3.15); PDF pp. 37-38, eqs. (A.4)-(A.9).)

undebatable_constraints: Flexible Theorem 3.4 fixes one M_R for all iterations/columns; permitting independently varying M_R^{(j)} would contradict the selected source. (PDF p. 12, Section 3.4 opening.)
Both selected variants have M_L≡I and a nonidentity right preconditioner M_R. (PDF p. 11, Section 3.3 opening; PDF p. 12, Section 3.4 opening.)
Equation (3.14), including its Frobenius-norm bound and its quantification over column applications, is inherited by both variants. (PDF pp. 11-12, eq. (3.14) and Section 3.4.)
rho_A^R must retain its componentwise-absolute numerator and cancellation-sensitive denominator exactly as in (3.15). (PDF p. 11, eq. (3.15).)
All five entries of (3.16) belong to Theorem 3.3's applicability condition. (PDF p. 11, eq. (3.16).)
Theorem 3.4 assumes the same full condition (3.16), including u_m eta_R κ(M_R)≪1, despite omitting the corresponding explicit term from (3.20). (PDF p. 12, Theorem 3.4 and Remark 5.)
The right bound must contain exactly the three displayed contributions u_g κ(A M_R^{-1})κ(M_R), u_m eta_R κ(M_R), and u_a κ(A)rho_A^R under one outer c(n,k). (PDF p. 11, eq. (3.17).)
The flexible bound must contain the first and third right-bound contributions under one outer c(n,k), with no explicit u_m eta_R κ(M_R) summand. (PDF p. 12, eq. (3.20).)

Theorem 3.4 does not logically require existence of a right-preconditioned witness from Theorem 3.3; its proof directly reuses shared perturbation results. (PDF p. 12, text before Theorem 3.4; PDF pp. 44-45, Appendix D.)

Right solution formation reapplies M_R^{-1} after forming V_hat_k y_hat_k, while flexible solution formation uses the persistently stored Z_hat_k without reapplication. (PDF p. 11, Section 3.3; PDF p. 12, Section 3.4.)

Remark 4 supports only an approximate-bound comparison and omission of a perturbation contribution; it does not state an exact algebraic identity or repeal any theorem hypothesis. (PDF p. 12, Remark 4; PDF p. 45, eq. (D.2).)

The existential dimension comes from the MGS/Theorem 3.1 mechanism and its conditioning property, not from assuming the other algorithm variant succeeds. (PDF p. 36, Appendix A opening; PDF p. 44, Appendix C conclusion.)
The Appendix C and D perturbation decompositions are locally derived proof facts, not theorem assumptions to be independently quantified. (PDF pp. 41-45, Appendices C-D.)

The unqualified κ in the displayed theorems must not silently be replaced by a uniquely specified κ_2 or κ_F without recording an interpretive choice. (PDF p. 6, norm conventions; PDF pp. 11-12, theorem formulas.)
The symbols ≲, ≈, and ≪ are qualitative source conventions; the selected claims are not exact real inequalities with explicit constants or remainders. (PDF p. 6, Section 2 conventions.)

ambiguities.issue: The k-dependent applicability condition is written before the existential k is introduced.
ambiguities.evidence: Equation (3.16) contains rho_A^R defined from Z_hat_k and y_hat_k, yet Theorem 3.3 says to assume (3.16) and only afterward says there exists k≤n; Theorem 3.4 repeats that form. Appendix C instead reasons at an arbitrary k satisfying (3.7) and then invokes the MGS existence result. (PDF p. 11, eqs. (3.15)-(3.17); PDF p. 12, Theorem 3.4; PDF pp. 41 and 44, Appendix C opening and conclusion.)
ambiguities.impact: The PDF does not cleanly distinguish among a condition at the selected witness, existence of a witness satisfying both the MGS property and (3.16), or uniform validity over every MGS-admissible candidate. A formalization must record this scope issue rather than silently impose a universal condition or detach (3.16) from the witness.

ambiguities.issue: Remark 4's phrase remove the dependence on u_m is stronger than the literal theorem contract.
ambiguities.evidence: The displayed flexible bound has no explicit u_m summand, but Theorem 3.4 still assumes (3.16), which contains u_m eta_R κ(M_R), and rho_A^R is built from Z_hat_k whose columns were computed in u_m. (PDF p. 11, eqs. (3.14)-(3.16); PDF p. 12, Theorem 3.4 and Remark 4.)
ambiguities.impact: The defensible logical claim is absence of the explicit preconditioner-reapplication term from the displayed first-order bound, not complete functional or applicability independence from u_m.

ambiguities.issue: The condition-number norm is intentionally left unresolved.
ambiguities.evidence: Section 2 defines κ_F, κ_2, and κ_{F,2} and then says it simply writes κ when norm equivalence makes differentiation unnecessary; all selected formulas use this unqualified κ. (PDF p. 6, norm conventions; PDF pp. 11-12, eqs. (3.16), (3.17), and (3.20).)
ambiguities.impact: An exact formal statement must choose norms and potentially dimension-dependent equivalence constants, but that choice is not fixed by the source.

ambiguities.issue: The asymptotic comparison symbols have no quantitative semantics.
ambiguities.evidence: The paper defines ≲ and ≈ by dropping negligible second-order terms and uses ≪ qualitatively, with no threshold, hidden constant, or explicit remainder. (PDF p. 6, Section 2 conventions.)
ambiguities.impact: The bounds and applicability conditions cannot be translated into exact inequalities without adding a semantics absent from the PDF.

ambiguities.issue: Nonzero denominators used in rho_A^R and Appendix A are not separately assumed.
ambiguities.evidence: Equation (3.15) divides by ||Z_hat_k y_hat_k||_2. Appendix A defines x_hat_k^R=M_R Z_tilde_k y_hat_k and divides by its norm; the later well-definedness statement cites full rank of M_R Z_tilde_k but does not state y_hat_k≠0. (PDF p. 11, eq. (3.15); PDF pp. 37-38, eqs. (A.4)-(A.9).)
ambiguities.impact: Satisfaction of (3.16) implicitly presupposes a finite defined rho_A^R, but the theorem omits an explicit nonvacuity assumption. Full column rank alone does not exclude a zero image when y_hat_k=0.

ambiguities.issue: Algorithm 1 has a residual-sign and initial-guess mismatch with its least-squares update and with Algorithm 2.
ambiguities.evidence: Algorithm 1 defines r_0=A x_0-b, minimizes ||beta e_1-H_bar_k y||_2, and adds the correction to x_0. With that residual sign, an additive correction naturally produces beta e_1+H_bar_k y. Algorithm 2 instead minimizes ||b_tilde-C_k y||_2 and forms x_k=Z_tilde_k y without x_0. (PDF p. 4, Algorithm 1 lines 1-18; PDF p. 7, Algorithm 2.)
ambiguities.impact: The source does not say whether r_0 should be b-Ax_0, whether the correction should be subtracted, or whether the theorem proof silently specializes to x_0=0 or to a correction equation. A formal algorithm-level contract must expose this inconsistency.

ambiguities.issue: The full-rank and no-breakdown premises needed by the modular theorem are not restated in Theorems 3.3 and 3.4.
ambiguities.evidence: Theorem 3.1 assumes a full-rank basis of increasing dimension, and the MGS model requires numerical nonsingularity. The selected theorem statements mention only the algorithm, nonsingular system, and (3.16). Appendix C later derives rank estimates while already working at a k satisfying (3.7). (PDF pp. 7-8, MGS model and Theorem 3.1; PDF pp. 11-12, Theorems 3.3-3.4; PDF pp. 42-44, eqs. (C.9)-(C.15).)
ambiguities.impact: It is unclear whether these premises are intended as inherited algorithmic regularity assumptions, consequences of (3.16), or silently excluded breakdown cases.

ambiguities.issue: The existential MGS result is imported and generalized without a local proof.
ambiguities.evidence: Appendix A recalls [11, eqs. (5.15)-(5.17)], notes that the cited reasoning was for Z_tilde_k≡V_hat_k and M_L≡I, and says it can be straightforwardly adapted to the broader setting. (PDF p. 36, Appendix A opening.)
ambiguities.impact: The selected PDF states the generalized MGS existence fact but does not independently establish it; its validity is an imported dependency rather than a locally derived source claim.

ambiguities.issue: Exceptional floating-point behavior is not specified.
ambiguities.evidence: The paper cites the standard floating-point model but does not spell out assumptions concerning overflow, underflow, special values, or zero normalization factors. (PDF p. 5, Section 2; PDF p. 4, Algorithm 1.)
ambiguities.impact: A machine-level formalization must either import the external standard model's exclusions or add explicit exceptional-value assumptions not present in the PDF.

contract_plain_english: For each variant, the paper studies a nonsingular real system with M_L=I and one fixed nonsingular nonidentity M_R. Every preconditioned column is computed under (3.14), A is applied in u_a, and the MGS work is performed in u_g. Right GMRES forms V_hat_k y_hat_k and reapplies M_R^{-1}; flexible GMRES stores Z_hat_k and forms Z_hat_k y_hat_k directly. (PDF pp. 11-12, Sections 3.3-3.4.) Under all five qualitative smallness requirements in (3.16), Theorem 3.3 separately asserts an existential right bound with three contributions, while Theorem 3.4 separately asserts an existential flexible bound omitting only the explicit u_m eta_R κ(M_R) reapplication contribution; c(n,k) multiplies each whole sum. (PDF p. 11, eqs. (3.16)-(3.17); PDF p. 12, eq. (3.20).) The flexible theorem does not require a right-theorem witness, and Remark 4 is a comparison of first-order bounds, not an exact identity or a weakening of (3.16). (PDF p. 12, Theorem 3.4 and Remark 4; PDF pp. 44-45, Appendix D.) The witness k is obtained through an imported MGS existence result and local Appendix C/D perturbation propagation, with unresolved scope, norm, denominator, residual-sign, higher-order, and exceptional-value issues as recorded above. (PDF p. 36, Appendix A; PDF pp. 41-45, Appendices C-D.)
